items.label: Her rights and the notice rule explained

objective: Explain confidentiality and privileged communication, their limits, and how HIPAA protects health information
secondaryObjectives: Keep accurate, relevant records and bill only for services provided, by the person who provided them

sources.cite: RCW 70.02.060 (1991 c 335 s 205): before serving a discovery request or compulsory process for health care information, the requester gives the provider and the patient advance notice with a date to seek a protective order, 'in no event' less than fourteen days; without that notice, 'Without the written consent of the patient, the health care provider may not disclose'; complying does not waive any privilege
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the Legislature's PDF of the section (summarizing fetch with the short quotes given).

sources.cite: HHS, HIPAA FAQ 706, What satisfactory assurances must a covered entity receive before it responds to a subpoena? A subpoena not accompanied by a court order allows disclosure only with written satisfactory assurances that the individual was given notice and the time to object passed, or that a qualified protective order was sought (45 CFR 164.512(e))
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on hhs.gov (summarizing fetch with short quotes).

brief.situation: You are a licensed independent clinical social worker in private practice in Washington. Karen Liu, 36 (a fictional client), has seen you for six months for depression after her divorce. This morning a subpoena arrived from her ex-husband's attorney for 'any and all records' of her treatment, for a custody modification hearing, to be produced in ten days. It is a subpoena signed by the attorney, not an order signed by a judge, and nothing with it shows that Karen was given notice. Karen's session is now. You have 50 minutes.
handover: Your record: intake, a treatment plan, dated progress notes (some quoting her about her anger at her ex-husband), and billing.
Karen has a family-law attorney for the custody case.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Karen answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say. What she tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "Okay. Tired. The custody stuff is starting again. Mark wants the kids every other week now."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Karen nods. "Yeah. It's exhausting. I'm trying to stay calm for the kids."

tellHer.label: Tell her about the subpoena that came this morning: who sent it, what it asks for, and that nothing has been sent

effects.log: You tell Karen about the subpoena and that you have not released anything.

effects.finding: She goes pale. "All my records? Everything I said about him? He'll use it to say I'm unstable."

effects.log: Clients are told, when feasible, before information is disclosed and of its likely consequences (NASW 1.07(d)).

hearWishes.label: Ask what she wants to happen, and what she is most afraid of
hearWishes.available: not talking and (toldHer and not wishesHeard)

effects.log: You ask what she wants and what she fears.

effects.finding: "I don't want any of it going to him. I said things here I'd never say in court. I was angry. That's what therapy is for."

explainRights.label: Explain her rights plainly: you will not send records without her written authorization or a court order; Washington requires notice to her with time to seek a protective order; she can object
explainRights.available: not talking and (toldHer and not rightsExplained)

effects.log: You explain what the law requires before records can be released and what she can do.

effects.finding: "So it's not automatic. I can fight it."

effects.log: Under RCW 70.02.060, without notice to her and time to seek a protective order, a provider may not disclose without her written consent; HIPAA needs satisfactory assurances or a court order (45 CFR 164.512(e)).

suggestAttorney.label: Suggest she call her family-law attorney today about objecting or seeking a protective order
suggestAttorney.available: not talking and (toldHer and not attorneySuggested)

effects.log: You suggest she bring her attorney in now.

effects.finding: "I'll call Ms. Patel from the car."

explainCourtOrder.label: Explain what happens if a judge does order release: you would ask the court to limit it to what is necessary, or to keep the records sealed
explainCourtOrder.available: not talking and (rightsExplained and not courtOrderExplained)

effects.log: You explain what you would do if a court ordered disclosure.

effects.finding: "So even then you'd fight to keep it narrow. Okay."

effects.log: If a court orders disclosure that could harm her, ask the court to withdraw or narrow the order or to keep the records under seal (NASW 1.07(j)).

promiseNever.label: Promise her that her records will never be seen by anyone
promiseNever.available: not talking and (toldHer and not promisedNever)

effects.log: You promise that no one will ever see her records.
A court can order disclosure; promising it can never happen sets her up to feel betrayed.

dismiss.label: Tell her not to worry, judges rarely care about therapy notes
dismiss.available: not talking and (toldHer and not dismissedFear)

effects.log: You tell her not to worry about it.

effects.finding: "Easy for you to say. You're not the one he's trying to take the kids from."

blameHer.label: Point out that she might have been more careful about what she said in sessions
blameHer.available: not talking and (toldHer and not blamed)

effects.log: You suggest she should have been more careful in what she said.

effects.finding: "This was the one place I was supposed to be able to say it."

keepFromHer.label: Decide not to mention the subpoena to her, so she does not worry, and handle it yourself
keepFromHer.available: not talking and (not toldHer and not keptSecret)

effects.log: You keep the subpoena to yourself this session.

effects.finding: The session goes on about her week.

effects.log: She is the one whose information and privilege are at stake; she needs to know so she can object.
You close the session.

consult.label: Consult your liability carrier's risk line (or an attorney) before you respond

effects.log: The risk line agrees: respond in writing, produce nothing without her written authorization or a court order, and note that the notice the statute requires was not shown.

sendRecords.label: Send the complete record to the attorney today, to be safe

effects.log: You mail the full record to Mark's attorney.
Without notice to her, her written consent or a court order, this disclosure is not allowed (RCW 70.02.060; 45 CFR 164.512(e)).

callEx.label: Call Mark's attorney to explain that Karen is doing well and the records would not help him

effects.log: You discuss Karen's treatment with the opposing attorney.
Even a reassuring summary discloses her health information without authorization.

editNotes.label: Tidy the progress notes first: soften the quotes about her anger

effects.log: You rewrite three notes.
Altering records after a subpoena is falsifying them: never change a record to change what a court will see.

options.label: A written response to the attorney: no records without her written authorization or a court order; the required notice to her not shown; she is seeking a protective order through counsel
Left exactly as written; nothing added or altered

effects.log: Documented: response {responseDoc}, record {recordDoc}.

Karen says she cannot trust anyone, picks up her keys and leaves before the hour is over.

subpoena.title: Predict (not scored)
subpoena.context: A subpoena signed by the other side's attorney, not a judge, asks for all of Karen's records in ten days, with nothing showing she was told. What does it require of you?

choices.label: A response, not production: tell her, and release nothing without her written authorization or a court order

effects.log: Prediction: respond, do not produce.

choices.feedback: Right. A subpoena must be answered, but it is not a court order. In Washington the requester must give her notice and time to seek a protective order (RCW 70.02.060), and HIPAA needs satisfactory assurances or a court order (45 CFR 164.512(e)). Tell her first (NASW 1.07(d)).

choices.label: Send the records: a subpoena is a legal order

effects.log: Prediction: produce.

choices.feedback: A subpoena signed by an attorney is not a judge's order. Producing her records without notice to her, her consent or a court order breaks confidentiality.

choices.label: Ignore it: therapy records are confidential

effects.log: Prediction: ignore it.

choices.feedback: Confidential, but a subpoena still needs a timely response; ignoring it can bring sanctions. Respond, and protect her information while you do.

formulation.question: Write your formulation: what the subpoena does and does not require, what you told Karen, and how you responded.

parts.label: The law
parts.criteria: A subpoena is not a court order; Washington requires advance notice to the patient with at least 14 days to seek a protective order, and without it no disclosure without her written consent (RCW 70.02.060); HIPAA requires satisfactory assurances or a court order (45 CFR 164.512(e)); respond, do not ignore; if a court orders release, ask to narrow it or seal the records (NASW 1.07(j)).
parts.modelAnswer: The subpoena is signed by Mark's attorney, not a judge. Under RCW 70.02.060 he must give Karen notice and at least fourteen days to seek a protective order; nothing shows that happened, so I may not disclose without her written consent. HIPAA likewise needs satisfactory assurances or a court order. I will respond in writing rather than ignore it. If a judge later orders release, I will ask the court to limit it or seal the records (NASW 1.07(j)).

parts.label: Karen and the record
parts.criteria: Told her first and heard her wishes (NASW 1.07(d)); explained her rights and what a court could still do, with no promise it never will; her attorney involved; consultation; nothing said to the other side; the record left exactly as written.
parts.modelAnswer: I told Karen about the subpoena at the start, heard that she objects, and explained her rights and what a court could still order, without promising that no one will ever see her records. She is calling her attorney today about a protective order. I consulted my carrier's risk line. I said nothing to the other side, and the record stays exactly as written: altering it now would be falsifying it.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.
Not used by this case's endings: the case is judged on the response and the record.

protected.headline: Good: confidentiality protected, and the law followed
protected.body: You told her first, released nothing, explained what the subpoena does and does not require, involved her attorney, consulted, answered in writing, and left the record alone.

gaps.headline: Protected, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria below show what was missing.

walkout.headline: She left
walkout.body: Brushing off her fear about her children leaves her alone with the most frightening part of the custody case.

breach.headline: Her records went to the other side
breach.body: An attorney's subpoena is not a court order. Without notice to her and time to object, or her written consent, Washington law bars disclosure (RCW 70.02.060), and HIPAA needs assurances or an order (45 CFR 164.512(e)).

altered.headline: The record was altered
altered.body: Records are kept accurately and never changed to shape what a court sees. Add a dated note if something needs clarifying; never rewrite.

scoring.modelReasoning: A subpoena signed by an attorney is not a court order. It must be answered, but in Washington the requester must give the patient notice and at least fourteen days to seek a protective order, and without that the provider may not disclose without her written consent (RCW 70.02.060); HIPAA requires satisfactory assurances or a court order (45 CFR 164.512(e)). Tell Karen at the start (NASW 1.07(d)), hear her wishes, explain her rights and what a court could still order, and involve her attorney. Consult, respond in writing without producing anything, say nothing to the other side, and leave the record exactly as written. If a judge orders release, ask the court to narrow it or seal the records (NASW 1.07(j)).
